lines.text: Your CAPTCHA is hard because you are not passing a test. You are working for something bigger.

The original reCAPTCHA, built by Luis von Ahn at Carnegie Mellon and acquired by Google in September 2009, was explicitly dual purpose: block the bots and use the answers to digitize text OCR could not read.
A pair of words came back to you: a control word the system already knew, and an unknown word from a page the computer failed to read.
Your job was to prove you are human. The second word was a side door: every time someone read a hard word, the system recorded that answer as evidence about what the scan said.
By 2011 and 2012, the New York Times archive — back to 1851 — had been digitized this way, along with the older corpus from the New York Times request in 2007.
In 2012 the system began mixing in photographs of house numbers taken from Google Street View.
Google announced it was using the general public to read house numbers for its maps product.
So what did you become? You became the labelling engine. The CAPTCHA verifies you; the words you read feed the machine.
Why do captchas get harder over time? More pages are scanned, more words fail OCR, so the gap between easy and hard words grows — difficulty scales with how much labelling is still needed.
That is the whole trick. The modern image-grid version behaves the same way: the pictures you categorize become training data for the next version of the system.
Now the nuance, because it matters: we cannot prove that every individual puzzle you solved trained on your click — Google has never published what a specific challenge does.
What the documented design and history show is dual purpose, from the primary sources.
The difficulty scaling is the measurable claim we can make: difficulty tracks the amount of labelling still to be done, not how suspicious you look.
A yellow warning: the street-view era was documented, but v2 and v3 came later and their internals are not published.
One more honest note: CAPTCHA's impact is greatest for text-based challenges. The difficulty direction is stable.
Sources: Wikipedia on reCAPTCHA; CMU News, September 2009; The New York Times, 2011; The Register, April 2012.
Credits: Luis von Ahn, David Abraham, Manuel Blum, Colin McMillen, Ben Maurer, Edison Tan, Carnegie Mellon University.
